question.text: A train travels a distance of 480 km at a uniform speed. If the speed had been 8 km/h less, then it would have taken 3 hours more to cover the same distance. Find the speed of the train.

Time at usual speed = 480/x, time at reduced speed = 480/(x − 8).
480/x − 480/(x − 8) = 3
⇒ 480(x − 8) − 480x = 3x(x − 8)
⇒ −3840 = 3x² − 24x
⇒ 3x² − 24x + 3840 = 0
⇒ x² − 8x + 1280 = 0
⇒ (x − 40)(x + 32) = 0
⇒ x = 40 or x = −32. Speed cannot be negative.
∴ Speed of the train = 40 km/h.

question.text: (b) Why are decomposition reactions called the opposite of combination reactions? Write one chemical equation each for these two types of reactions mentioning the name of the reactant(s) and the product(s) involved in the reactions.

scheme.valuePoint: Combination: a single product formed from two or more reactants; decomposition: a single reactant breaks down into two or more products - so they are opposite
Example of combination reaction with names, e.g. C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + heat (carbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide)
Example of decomposition reaction with names, e.g. CaCO₃(s) →(heat) CaO(s) + CO₂(g) (calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide)
scheme.note: MS note p5: '(Do not deduct marks if physical state not given)'.

cases.text:
In a combination reaction two or more substances combine to form a single product, whereas in a decomposition reaction a single substance breaks down into two or more simpler products. Since one joins substances and the other breaks them apart, they are opposite to each other.
Combination: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (calcium oxide + water → calcium hydroxide)
Decomposition: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ on heating (calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide)

question.text: (a) (i) The power of a lens 'X' is −2.5 D. Name the lens and determine its focal length in cm. For which eye defect of vision will an optician prescribe this type of lens as a corrective lens? (ii) 'The value of magnification m for a lens is −2.' Using new Cartesian Sign Convention and considering that an object is placed at a distance of 20 cm from the optical centre of this lens, state: (I) the nature of the image formed; (II) size of the image compared to the size of the object; (III) position of the image, and (IV) sign of the height of the image. (iii) The numerical values of the focal lengths of two lenses A and B are 10 cm and 20 cm respectively. Which one of the two will show higher degree of convergence/divergence? Give reason to justify your answer.

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: lens type, focal length in cm, eye defect

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: m = −2: nature, size, position, sign of height

parts.label: (iii)
parts.text: which lens converges/diverges more, with reason

scheme.valuePoint: (I) real and inverted (II) magnified / double the size (III) beyond 2F on the other side (IV) negative
The lens with focal length 10 cm
Less focal length, more converging/diverging power

cases.text:
(i) Since the power is negative, X is a concave lens.
P = 1/f ⇒ f = 1/P = 1/(−2.5) = −4 m = −400 cm.
It is prescribed for myopia (short-sightedness).
(ii) m = −2 (negative) ⇒ (I) the image is real and inverted; (II) it is twice the size of the object (magnified); (III) v = m × u = (−2) × (−20) = +40 cm, i.e. 40 cm on the other side of the lens, beyond 2F; (IV) the height of the image is negative.
(iii) Lens A (f = 10 cm), because power P = 1/f — the shorter the focal length, the greater the power, i.e. the higher the degree of convergence/divergence.

perStep.reason: 1/(−2.5) = −0.4 m = −40 cm; the student wrote −4 m = −400 cm (decimal slip).
All four correct - (ii) is about a DIFFERENT lens (m = −2) and is independent of (i).

modelAnswerKeyFacts: real, inverted, magnified ×2, beyond 2F, negative height
expected.examinerNote: Science version of August defect 9: an early slip in (i) must not zero the independent parts (ii) and (iii). Decimal slip in 1/(−2.5) = performed wrongly = calculation; also a units conversion probe (m→cm).

question.text:
Study the food chain given below: Phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fishes → large fish
A. In the given food chain, the amount of energy available at the fourth trophic level is 10 kJ, what will be the energy available at the producer level?
B. Is it possible to have three more trophic levels in the above food chain? Justify.
C. Which of these trophic levels will have the maximum amount of pesticide, if it had washed down in the water body from agricultural fields. Why?

parts.label: A
parts.text: energy at producer level

parts.label: B
parts.text: three more trophic levels?

parts.label: C
parts.text: maximum pesticide

scheme.note: SQP MS prints only the question total (3); 1 + 1 + 1 per part is examiner judgement.

scheme.valuePoint: B. No - the loss of energy at each step is so much that very little usable energy will be left
C. Large fish, due to biological magnification of pesticide

cases.text:
A. By the 10% law only 10% of energy passes to the next level.
Large fish (4th level) = 10 kJ ⇒ small fishes = 100 kJ ⇒ zooplankton = 1000 kJ ⇒ phytoplankton = 1000 × 10 = 1,00,000 kJ.
B. No. At each trophic level about 90% of the energy is lost, so after three more levels very little usable energy would be left.
C. Large fish, because pesticides are non-biodegradable and accumulate at each trophic level (biological magnification), so the highest level has the maximum concentration.

perStep.reason: Method (10% law) right, but 1000 × 10 = 10,000 kJ, not 1,00,000 kJ.

question.text: In order to study patterns of inheritance, Neha had performed typical Mendelian experiments with pea plants in the field. In experiment one, she crossed a pea plant having white flowers (vv) with another pea plant bearing violet flowers (VV). In another experiment, in addition to the colour of the flower she also focussed on the height of the pea plant. This time she crossed a pea plant having violet flowers and tall height (VVTT) with another pea plant having white flowers and short height (vvtt). What percentage is expected for the following traits as a result of these experiments? Give a reason.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Violet flowers in F1 and F2 generation in experiment one?

parts.label: B
parts.text: Tall height plants with white flowers in F2 generation in experiment two?

parts.label: D
parts.text: Percentage of short height plants with white flowers in F1 and F2 generations in experiment two? [OR C: medium height plants with light violet flowers]

scheme.valuePoint: A. F1 100% violet (Vv); F2 75% violet (1/4 VV + 2/4 Vv) - violet is dominant
B. 3/16 or 18.75% tall with white flowers (vvTT/vvTt)
D. F1: 0% (all show dominant traits); F2: 1/16 or 6.25% short-white (vvtt), both recessive

cases.text:
A. Experiment one: F1 — 100% violet (Vv); F2 — 75% violet (VV and Vv), because violet is the dominant trait.
B. Tall plants with white flowers in F2 = 9/16, because tall is dominant.
D. F1: 0% short plants with white flowers, since all F1 plants (VvTt) show only the dominant traits. F2: 1/16 (6.25%) plants will be short with white flowers (vvtt), as both traits are recessive.

perStep.reason: 9/16 is the tall-VIOLET class; tall-white (vvT_) is 3/16.

expected.studentHeading: Marks to gain — learn this
commentMayMention: 9/16 is the proportion of tall violet plants; tall white is 3/16
expected.examinerNote: Confusing phenotype classes of the 9:3:3:1 ratio = method misunderstood = conceptual. Heredity is retained in 2026-27 - a grader or bank filter must not treat it as out of syllabus.
